{{Short description|Statistical measure in mathematical model}}

In [[statistics]], the '''variance inflation factor''' ('''VIF''') is the ratio ([[quotient]]) of the variance of a parameter estimate when fitting a full model that includes other parameters to the variance of the parameter estimate if the model is fit with only the parameter on its own.<ref>{{cite book |last1=James |first1=Gareth |last2=Witten |first2=Daniela |last3=Hastie |first3=Trevor |last4=Tibshirani |first4=Robert  |title=An Introduction to Statistical Learning |edition=8th |publisher=Springer Science+Business Media New York |year=2017 |isbn=978-1-4614-7138-7 }}</ref> The VIF provides an index that measures how much the [[variance]] (the square of the estimate's [[standard deviation]]) of an estimated regression coefficient is increased because of [[collinearity]]. 

[[Cuthbert Daniel]] claims to have invented the concept behind the variance inflation factor, but did not come up with the name.<ref>{{cite tech report |last=Snee |first=Ron |title=Origins of the Variance Inflation Factor as Recalled by Cuthbert Daniel |location= |publisher=Snee Associates |year=1981 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/291808767_Who_Invented_the_Variance_Inflation_Factor}}</ref>

==Definition==
Consider the following [[linear model]] with ''k'' independent variables:
: ''Y'' = ''β''<sub>0</sub> + ''β''<sub>1</sub> ''X''<sub>1</sub> + ''β''<sub>2</sub> ''X'' <sub>2</sub> + ... + ''β''<sub>''k''</sub> ''X''<sub>''k''</sub> + ''ε''.

The [[Standard error (statistics)|standard error]] of the estimate of ''β''<sub>''j''</sub> is the [[square root]] of the ''j''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1 diagonal element of ''s''<sup>2</sup>(''X''&prime;''X'')<sup>&minus;1</sup>, where ''s'' is the [[Root-mean-square deviation|root mean squared error (RMSE)]] (note that RMSE<sup>2</sup> is a [[consistent estimator]] of the true variance of the error term, <math> \sigma^2 </math>); ''X'' is the regression [[design matrix]] &mdash; a matrix such that ''X''<sub>''i'', ''j''+1</sub> is the value of the ''j''<sup>th</sup> [[Dependent and independent variables|independent variable]] for the ''i''<sup>th</sup> case or observation, and such that ''X''<sub>''i'',1</sub>, the predictor vector associated with [[The Intercept|the intercept]] term, equals 1 for all ''i''.  It turns out that the square of this standard error, the estimated variance of the estimate of ''β''<sub>''j''</sub>, can be equivalently expressed as:<ref>{{Cite book |title=Applied regression analysis : a research tool |url=https://archive.org/details/appliedregressio00rawl_492 |url-access=limited |last1=Rawlings|first1=John O.|date=1998|publisher=Springer|last2=Pantula |first2=Sastry G. |last3=Dickey |first3=David A. |isbn=0387227539|edition=Second |location=New York|pages=[https://archive.org/details/appliedregressio00rawl_492/page/n384 372], 373|oclc=54851769}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|url=https://cran.r-project.org/doc/contrib/Faraway-PRA.pdf|title=Practical Regression and Anova using R|last=Faraway|first=Julian J.|year=2002|pages=117, 118}}</ref>

:<math>
\widehat{\operatorname{var}}(\hat{\beta}_j) = \frac{s^2}{(n-1)\widehat{\operatorname{var}}(X_j)}\cdot \frac{1}{1-R_j^2},
</math>

where ''R''<sub>''j''</sub><sup>2</sup> is the [[coefficient of determination|multiple ''R''<sup>2</sup>]] for the regression of ''X''<sub>''j''</sub> on the other covariates (a regression that does not involve the response variable ''Y'') and  <math>\hat{\beta}_j</math> are the coefficient estimates, id est, the estimates of  <math>{\beta}_j</math>.  This identity separates the influences of several distinct factors on the variance of the coefficient estimate:

* ''s''<sup>2</sup>: greater scatter in the data around the regression surface leads to proportionately more variance in the coefficient estimates
* ''n'': greater sample size results in proportionately less variance in the coefficient estimates
* <math>\widehat\operatorname{var}(X_j)</math>: greater variability in a particular covariate leads to proportionately less variance in the corresponding coefficient estimate

The remaining term, 1&nbsp;/&nbsp;(1&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;''R''<sub>''j''</sub><sup>2</sup>) is the VIF.  It reflects all other factors that influence the uncertainty in the coefficient estimates.  The VIF equals 1 when the vector ''X''<sub>''j''</sub> is [[orthogonal]] to each column of the design matrix for the regression of ''X''<sub>''j''</sub> on the other covariates. By contrast, the VIF is greater than 1 when the vector ''X''<sub>''j''</sub> is not orthogonal to all columns of the design matrix for the regression of ''X''<sub>''j''</sub> on the other covariates.  Finally, note that the VIF is invariant to the scaling of the variables (that is, we could scale each variable ''X''<sub>''j''</sub> by a constant ''c''<sub>''j''</sub> without changing the VIF).

:<math>
\widehat{\operatorname{var}}(\hat{\beta}_j) = s^2 [(X^T X)^{-1}]_{jj}
</math>
Now let <math>r= X^T X</math>, and without losing generality, we reorder the columns of ''X'' to set the first column to be <math>X_j</math>
:<math>
r^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} r_{j,j} & r_{j,-j} \\ r_{-j,j} & r_{-j,-j}\end{bmatrix}^{-1}
</math>

: <math> r_{j,j} = X_j^T X_j, r_{j,-j} = X_j^T X_{-j}, r_{-j,j} = X_{-j}^T X_j, r_{-j,-j} = X_{-j}^T X_{-j}</math>.

By using [[Schur complement]], the element in the first row and first column in <math> r^{-1} </math> is, 
:<math>r^{-1}_{1,1} = [r_{j,j} - r_{j,-j} r_{-j,-j}^{-1} r_{-j,j} ]^{-1} </math>
Then we have, 
:<math>
\begin{align}
& \widehat{\operatorname{var}}(\hat{\beta}_j) = s^2 [(X^T X)^{-1}]_{jj} = s^2 r^{-1}_{1,1} \\
= {} & s^2 [X_j^T X_j - X_j^T X_{-j} (X_{-j}^T X_{-j})^{-1} X_{-j}^T X_j ]^{-1} \\ 
= {} & s^2 [X_j^T X_j - X_j^T X_{-j} (X_{-j}^T X_{-j})^{-1} (X_{-j}^T X_{-j}) (X_{-j}^T X_{-j})^{-1} X_{-j}^T X_j ]^{-1} \\
= {} & s^2 [X_j^T X_j -  \hat{\beta}_{*j}^T(X_{-j}^T X_{-j}) \hat{\beta}_{*j} ]^{-1} \\
= {} & s^2 \frac{1}{\mathrm{RSS}_j} \\
= {} & \frac{s^2}{(n-1)\widehat\operatorname{var}(X_j)}\cdot \frac{1}{1-R_j^2}
\end{align}
</math>
Here <math> \hat{\beta}_{*j} </math> is the coefficient of regression of dependent variable <math>X_j </math> over covariate <math>X_{-j} </math>. <math>\mathrm{RSS}_j </math> is the corresponding [[residual sum of squares]].

==Calculation and analysis==

We can calculate ''k'' different VIFs (one for each ''X''<sub>''i''</sub>) in three steps:

=== Step one ===
First we run an ordinary least square regression that has ''X''<sub>''i''</sub> as a function of all the other explanatory variables in the first equation.<br /> If ''i'' = 1, for example,  equation would be
:<math>X_1=\alpha_0 + \alpha_2 X_2 + \alpha_3 X_3 + \cdots + \alpha_k X_k +\varepsilon</math>

where <math>\alpha_0</math> is a constant and <math>\varepsilon</math> is the [[errors and residuals in statistics|error term]].

=== Step two ===

Then, calculate the VIF factor for <math>\hat\alpha_i</math> with the following formula :

: <math>\mathrm{VIF}_i = \frac{1}{1-R^2_i}</math>

where ''R''<sup>2</sup><sub>''i''</sub> is the [[coefficient of determination]] of the regression equation in step one, with <math> X_i </math> on the left hand side, and all other predictor variables (all the other X variables) on the right hand side.

=== Step three ===
Analyze the magnitude of [[multicollinearity]] by considering the size of the <math>\operatorname{VIF}(\hat \alpha_i)</math>. A [[rule of thumb]] is that if <math>\operatorname{VIF}(\hat \alpha_i) > 10</math> then multicollinearity is high<ref>{{cite book |last1=Kutner |first1=M. H. |last2=Nachtsheim |first2=C. J. |last3=Neter |first3=J. |title=Applied Linear Regression Models |edition=4th |publisher=McGraw-Hill Irwin |year=2004 }}</ref> (a cutoff of 5 is also commonly used<ref name="Sheather 2009 p. ">{{cite book | last=Sheather | first=Simon | title=A modern approach to regression with R | publisher=Springer | publication-place=New York, NY | year=2009 | isbn=978-0-387-09607-0 }}</ref>). However, there is no value of VIF greater than 1 in which the variance of the slopes of predictors isn't inflated. As a result, including two or more variables in a multiple regression that are not orthogonal (i.e. have correlation = 0), will alter each other's slope, SE of the slope, and [[P-value]], because there is shared variance between the predictors that can't be uniquely attributed to any one of them.<ref>{{cite book |last1=James |first1=Gareth |last2=Witten |first2=Daniela |last3=Hastie |first3=Trevor |last4=Tibshirani |first4=Robert |title=An introduction to statistical learning: with applications in R |date=2021 |publisher=Springer |location=New York, NY |isbn=978-1-0716-1418-1 |page=116 |edition=Second |doi=10.1007/978-1-0716-1418-1 |url=https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-1-0716-1418-1 |access-date=1 November 2024}}</ref>

Some software instead calculates the tolerance which is just the reciprocal of the VIF. The choice of which to use is a matter of personal preference.

== Interpretation ==
The square root of the variance inflation factor indicates how much larger the standard error increases compared to if that variable had 0 correlation to other predictor variables in the model.

'''Example'''<br />
If the variance inflation factor of a predictor variable were 5.27 (√5.27&nbsp;=&nbsp;2.3), this means that the standard error for the coefficient of that predictor variable is 2.3 times larger than if that predictor variable had 0 correlation with the other predictor variables.

== Implementation ==

*<code>vif</code> function in the [https://cran.r-project.org/package=car car] [[R (programming language)|R]] package
*<code>ols_vif_tol</code> function in the [https://cran.r-project.org/package=olsrr olsrr] [[R (programming language)|R]] package
*<code>PROC REG</code> in SAS [https://support.sas.com/documentation/cdl/en/statug/63033/HTML/default/viewer.htm#statug_reg_sect007.htm System]
*<code>variance_inflation_factor</code> function in [http://www.statsmodels.org statsmodels] [[Python (programming language)|Python]] package
*<code>estat vif</code> in [https://www.stata.com/help.cgi?regress_postestimation Stata]
*[https://grass.osgeo.org/grass78/manuals/addons/r.vif.html r.vif] addon for [[GRASS GIS]]
*<code>vif</code> (non categorical) and <code>gvif</code> (categorical data) functions in [https://juliastats.org/StatsModels.jl/stable/ StatsModels] [[Julia (programming language)|Julia]] programing language
